column3: The immediately preceding request names Gog and Magog's corruption, proposes payment, and asks for the very barrier that the focus answers.
It introduces the Dhul-Qarnayn account whose final journey supplies the focus's model of enabled leadership.
The replacement of a harmful child with a better one does not clarify collaborative protection or public works.
Noah asks for judgment and salvation with the believers, a distant collective-protection parallel.
The immediate continuation specifies the community-built barrier through iron, fire, and molten copper.
The threatened ruin of a garden does not develop the focus's governance or construction response.
The command to hold revelation with strength supplies a limited parallel to the focus's call for strength.
It immediately confirms that the completed barrier defeats both climbing and breaching.
God's lordship over all worlds does not specifically illuminate the focus.
Iblis's boast and refusal to prostrate are unrelated to the protective work described here.
Dhul-Qarnayn attributes the barrier to divine mercy and states its eventual collapse by God's true promise.
Shu'ayb forbids corruption after reform, directly framing the social harm from which the focus protects a people.
The command to take what was given with strength parallels the focus's demand for capable participation.
It places Dhul-Qarnayn between the two mountains with the linguistically isolated community he will assist.
Human ingratitude does not explain the focus's public-protection action.
Yahya is commanded to take the Book with strength, a related but non-collective use of strength.
It grounds the focus's claim in God-given authority and access to means.
Pharaoh's question about Moses and Aaron's Lord has no meaningful link to the focus.
Its protection of noncombatants under treaty offers only a broad concern for avoiding harm between peoples.
The unpaid repair of a collapsing wall is a close narrative parallel to the focus's refusal of payment for protective construction.
The closing prayer for forgiveness and mercy does not develop the focus's themes.
Final divine judgment of disputes does not clarify the practical response in the focus.
Dhul-Qarnayn's following of a means begins the journey whose final stage reaches the focus.
A calculated reward from God is unrelated to communal construction or protection.
Moses is told to hold the tablets with strength and direct his people toward their best commands.
The believers' retreat to a cave is a different form of seeking safety under divine mercy.
Adhering to revelation does not directly address the focus's enabled governance or barrier.
Taking revelation with strength is present, but the verse centers on Israel's disobedience.
Dhul-Qarnayn is given a choice of punishment or good treatment for a people, establishing his just authority.
Glorification of the Lord does not clarify the focus.
Worldly provision being better and more lasting elsewhere does not relate to the focus's project.
The sleepers' protected cave setting offers only remote shelter imagery.
Iblis's enmity does not illuminate the response to Gog and Magog in the focus.
Abraham's prayer for a secure city directly supports the focus's public aim of protecting a community.
Dhul-Qarnayn's stated punishment of the wrongdoer establishes the just-ruler ethic immediately before the focus.
God's lordship of the heavens, earth, and horizons has no specific connection here.
God's replacement of what people spend only faintly relates to the refused payment in the focus.
God's protection and guidance of the cave companions is only a distant contextual parallel.
The magicians' confession of Moses and Aaron's Lord does not address the focus.
Mutual shelter, support, and striving among believers provide a broad parallel to collective assistance.
Dhul-Qarnayn promises good reward and ease of command to the righteous, completing his model of fair rule.
God's lordship and forgiveness do not develop the focus's themes.
Zechariah's sign of temporary silence is unrelated to public protection or shared labor.
The divinely directed repair of a wall protects orphans' property, a related protective-building motif.
Lasting righteous deeds over wealth offer a broad moral background for refusing material payment.
Divine judgment belongs to God, but the verse does not clarify the focus's practical action.
Dhul-Qarnayn again follows a means, carrying the journey toward the community in the focus.
The condemned seek increased punishment for a misleader, unrelated to the focus.
Treaty obligations in accidental-homicide compensation offer only a remote relation to relations between communities.
A people without shelter from the sunrise does not connect to the barrier or its construction.
The promised gardens for the God-conscious do not clarify the focus.
Moses directs his people to seek God's help and endure together under oppression, a broad communal-strength parallel.
God's encompassing knowledge of Dhul-Qarnayn's circumstances gives only local narrative background.
The reward of two gardens for fearing God is unrelated to the focus.
Moses's reliance on God's guidance during danger is a distant protection and leadership parallel.
Dhul-Qarnayn follows a means for the third time, directly leading to the focus's setting.
The magicians' faith and forgiveness concern a distinct response to coercion.
Shu'ayb's knowledge that God knows people's deeds does not clarify the focus.
Veiling from the Lord on Judgment Day has no substantive connection to the focus.
God grants people establishment and livelihoods on earth, paralleling the divine enabling claimed in the focus.
Obedience to legitimate authority and returning disputes to God and the Messenger provide a broad governance framework.
The request for an idol is unrelated to construction, communal effort, or protection.
Remembering selected prophets does not clarify the focus.
Zechariah's sign and remembrance instruction do not relate to the focus.
Abraham's submission to God does not address the focus's public works or leadership.
Earlier peoples' God-given establishment shows that power is granted by God, as the focus explicitly acknowledges.
The chosen status of prophets does not clarify the focus.
God's protection and elevation of Jesus and his followers offer only a broad security parallel.
Distinct responsibility for each community's deeds does not develop the focus.
God's knowledge of all speech does not clarify the focus's action.
The magicians' confession is unrelated to the focus.
The objection to monotheism does not connect to the focus.
The warning against harming the Prophet does not illuminate the focus's communal barrier.
The messenger's strength and rank give only a lexical, not thematic, parallel.
Striving with wealth and selves presents committed collective effort, though not the civic construction of the focus.
The specifications for the cow do not clarify the focus.
Return to God does not address the focus's themes.
Seeking God's judgment and help is a distant parallel to authoritative intervention.
The wish to delay death for charity does not clarify the focus.
Seeking help through patience and prayer is only a general counterpart to the focus's request for human strength.
Return to the Lord has no specific relevance here.
The secure resting place for a drop of fluid is unrelated to protective infrastructure.
Worship of the Lord of the House does not clarify the focus.
Seeking divine help is a broad contrast to the focus's request for the people's practical assistance.
Magnifying the Lord does not develop the focus.
The embryo's secure resting place is unrelated to the focus.
The reference to Aad does not clarify the focus's governance or barrier.
The separation of Moses and Khidr and explanation of hidden wisdom are only local narrative background.
God's lordship of the heavens and throne does not clarify the focus.
A hypocrite's regret at missing gain does not connect to the focus.
The contrast of hospitality and the tree of Zaqqum is unrelated to the focus.
Disputation before God does not clarify collaborative protection.
Gratitude for God's gifts and reform of descendants offer a broad ethical backdrop but no close link.
The Quran's descent from the Lord of all worlds does not clarify the focus's communal construction.
Moses's people ask not to be made a trial for wrongdoers, a remote protection-from-oppression parallel.
Glorification of the Lord does not clarify the focus.
Adam's naming of things and God's knowledge do not relate to the focus.
Moses's complaint about a criminal people does not develop the focus's response.
The question about cultivation is unrelated to the focus.
The prayer not to be placed among wrongdoers is only a broad appeal for protection.
The immediate sequel describes the released peoples surging together after the barrier's appointed end, completing its protective horizon.
It condemns those who claim to reform while spreading corruption on earth, directly naming the harm at issue in 18:94-95.
Talut's divinely granted kingship, knowledge, and physical capacity closely parallel authority and capability given to a just leader.
God's repelling some people through others prevents corruption on earth, directly grounding protective intervention against destructive aggression.
It mandates an organized community that calls to good, enjoins right, and restrains wrong, supporting collective social repair.
Consultation in public affairs gives a governance counterpart to mobilizing a community for a shared undertaking.
It commands rendering trusts and judging people with justice, a core norm for the authority exercised in the focus.
It calls for defending oppressed men, women, and children seeking rescue from an oppressive town, closely matching protection of a vulnerable people.
It explicitly commands cooperation in righteousness and God-consciousness while forbidding cooperation in sin and aggression.
It addresses those who wage war and spread corruption on earth, the violent social threat for which the focus builds protection.
The command to uphold justice even toward hostility anchors the focus's exercise of power in impartial justice.
It forbids corruption on earth after its reform, directly framing the focus's response to corrupting forces.
Moses appoints Harun to govern among his people, commands reform, and forbids the path of corrupters, a close leadership parallel.
It commands preparing available force to deter hostile enemies, directly paralleling the focus's material defense against a threat.
It warns that failure of mutual alliance and protection produces persecution and great corruption on earth.
It praises those who forbid corruption on earth among earlier generations, clarifying the social duty opposed to Gog and Magog's corruption.
The king recognizes Joseph as established and trusted, a related model of entrusted public authority.
Joseph requests oversight of the land's storehouses because he is knowing and guarding, a practical public-stewardship parallel.
God provides coats of mail to protect people from violence, a direct parallel in protective material technology.
Its command of justice, excellence, and care for kin provides a broad ethical framework for public leadership.
Moses asks for a helper from his own people, closely paralleling the focus's request for communal assistance.
Moses asks that his helper share his task, directly paralleling a leader who involves others in a necessary work.
God teaches David the making of protective armor for people in battle, an especially close parallel in divinely enabled defensive craftsmanship.
Permission to resist is given to those wronged, supplying the principle of defense against aggression.
It explains that God repels some people through others so places of worship are not destroyed, directly linking defense with protection of communities.
It promises believers establishment, authority, and security after fear, closely resonating with the focus's divinely enabled security project.
Solomon rejects a material gift because what God gave him is better, a close verbal and ethical parallel to Dhul-Qarnayn's refusal of payment.
The description of the best worker as strong and trustworthy closely matches the competence and integrity required by the focus.
Moses asks for Harun as a supporting helper, reinforcing the principle that a leader's mission is strengthened through capable assistance.
It attributes corruption on land and sea to what people have done, directly illuminating the focus's concern with earthly corruption.
God appoints guiding leaders when they are patient and certain, supplying a strong model of divinely grounded leadership.
God softens iron for David, a material antecedent to the ironwork used for the barrier in the focus.
David is commanded to make protective coats of mail and work righteously, closely pairing skilled fabrication with ethical responsibility.
David is made a vicegerent and commanded to judge justly rather than follow desire, a direct governance parallel.
Believers conduct their affairs by consultation, supporting the participatory public action in the focus.
It commands communal intervention and justice to stop armed aggression between groups, a close parallel to protection from violent threat.
It identifies iron as containing great might and benefit for people, directly supporting the focus's iron barrier.
The image of believers standing as a solid structure gives a distant image of disciplined collective strength.
